title: This product just launched and got a flash crowd of new users — how does your design cope?
summary: Distinct from a capacity-estimation question: this is about the architectural posture — queueing, waiting rooms, feature-flagged rollout — not the math of how big the spike is.

slides.markdown:
A flash crowd at launch is a different problem from steady 10x growth: it's sudden, often unpredictable in size, and hits a system with zero warm-up — no pre-scaled capacity, no warmed caches. The question is testing your **architectural posture**, not your capacity math.

By the end of this topic you'll be able to name the specific mechanisms — edge-level load shedding, gradual rollout, pre-warming — that protect a backend from a sudden crowd, rather than just saying "autoscaling will handle it."

slides.sectionTitle: Clarifying questions: is the launch timed, or could it go viral unpredictably?
slides.markdown:
Ask: is this a **scheduled launch** (a specific time, some ability to pre-scale and pre-warm) or could it **go viral unpredictably** (a social post takes off with no warning)? The two need different postures — a scheduled launch can pre-provision; an unpredictable one needs the system to defend itself reactively, in real time, with no advance notice.

This single question usually determines whether your answer leans on preparation or on runtime defenses.

slides.sectionTitle: The answer skeleton: shed load at the edge, roll out gradually
slides.markdown:
The skeleton: **shed load gracefully at the edge**, before it ever reaches the database or core services, and **roll out access gradually** rather than opening the doors to 100% of demand at once.

This is a different toolkit from the "scale to 10x" question — the emphasis isn't scaling the backend bigger, it's controlling *how much load the backend ever sees* in the first place, since backend capacity can't be conjured instantly no matter how well-designed it is.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: a virtual waiting room at the edge
slides.markdown:
A **virtual waiting room** sits in front of the real system and admits users at a controlled rate — everyone else sees a queue position and an estimated wait, rather than the backend being flooded and failing for everyone. It's the same principle ticket-sale sites use for high-demand launches.

The key property: it converts an uncontrolled surge into a controlled, predictable admission rate the backend was actually designed to handle — trading a visible queue for backend stability.

For a scheduled launch, **gradual rollout** — 1% of users, then 10%, then 100%, watching metrics at each step — catches capacity problems while the blast radius is still small, instead of discovering them the moment every user is let in at once.

The discipline here is patience: a launch that's going well at 1% still needs to actually be watched at each subsequent step, not rushed to 100% because the first step looked fine.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: pre-warming caches and connection pools before doors open
slides.markdown:
For a scheduled launch, **pre-warm** everything that's normally warmed by organic traffic: run synthetic load against caches so they aren't empty at t=0, and open connection pools to the database ahead of time so the first real users aren't all paying a cold-start connection cost simultaneously.

A cache or pool that's empty at launch behaves like a much smaller one for the first wave of real traffic — pre-warming removes that avoidable extra load right when the system can least afford it.

slides.sectionTitle: The trade-off to name out loud: a waiting room protects the backend, costs first impressions
slides.markdown:
| | With a waiting room | Without one |
|---|---|---|
| Backend stability | Protected — admission rate is controlled | At risk — uncontrolled surge can overload it |
| User experience | Some users wait, see a queue position | Everyone gets in immediately, if it holds |
| Failure mode if overwhelmed anyway | Degrades gracefully — queue grows, backend stays up | Can fail hard for everyone at once |

**How to decide:** a waiting room trades a visible, honest wait for a small fraction of users against the risk of a hard failure for everyone — for a high-stakes launch, that trade is usually worth it.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: the waiting room itself gets overwhelmed — what protects that?
slides.markdown:
This is the recursive version of the SPOF question: the waiting room must be **the cheapest, most horizontally-scalable thing you own**, since it's now the component absorbing the entire uncontrolled surge. It should do almost nothing per request — check a counter, maybe set a cookie — precisely so it can scale trivially and stay up even when everything behind it would have fallen over.

If the waiting room itself does real work (a database lookup per visitor, say), you've just moved the bottleneck one hop earlier instead of removing it.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: how do you know it's actually working, in real time?
slides.markdown:
Name the specific dashboards you'd have open live during the launch: **admission rate vs backend capacity** (are you letting people in faster than the backend can serve them), **backend error rate and latency** (is the admitted traffic actually succeeding), and **queue depth and wait-time estimate** (is the line growing faster than it's draining).

A launch "working" isn't a vibe — it's these numbers staying within planned bounds, watched live so you can throttle the admission rate down immediately if the backend starts to strain.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: relying on autoscaling alone with no edge gate
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** autoscaling alone will handle a launch flash crowd — just let the cluster grow with demand.

**Why it's wrong:** autoscaling reacts on a delay (new instances take time to boot, warm up, and join the pool), and a flash crowd can flood the system in seconds — well before new capacity is ready. Without a gate at the edge, the existing capacity gets overwhelmed during exactly that window.

**Correct model:** pair autoscaling with an edge-level admission control (a waiting room, rate limiting) that buys the time autoscaling needs to actually catch up. See [graceful degradation and load shedding](graceful-degradation-and-load-shedding) for the underlying mechanics.
